why: Because walks may revisit roads, any road in the connected component that holds city 1 (and city n) can be stepped onto. The answer is just the smallest road distance inside that component: union all roads, then take the min over roads whose endpoint has city 1's root.
hints: Revisiting is allowed. What does that let a path do with a cheap road far away from the direct route?
Any road reachable from city 1 can be walked to and back, and city n is in the same component. So the score is the minimum distance over every road in city 1's component, not a shortest-path problem.
Union both ends of every road, then scan the roads once and keep the smallest distance whose endpoint shares city 1's root. O((n + m) α(n)) time; a BFS or DFS from city 1 works just as well.
pitfalls: This is not Dijkstra: the score is a minimum along a walk, not a sum, and revisits are free.
Roads in other components must be ignored even if they are cheaper.
Cities are numbered 1..n, so size the parent array n+1.
constraints:
• 2 <= n <= 10^5
  • 1 <= roads.length <= 10^5
  • roads[i] = [a, b, distance], 1 <= a, b <= n, a != b
  • 1 <= distance <= 10^4
  • At most one road between any two cities; at least one path between city 1 and city n exists.
  • Bounds are not stated in the source; these are the canonical problem's bounds.
